title: NEB Class 11 Physics — Solids — 2022
subject: physics
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: What is an intrinsic semiconductor? Define electrons and holes as charge carriers.
questions.solution:
**Intrinsic semiconductor:** Pure semiconductor material without any impurities (e.g., pure silicon or germanium).

**Electron:** A negatively charged charge carrier promoted to the conduction band.
**Hole:** The positively charged vacancy left in the valence band when an electron leaves. Holes move in the direction of electric field.
questions.knowledgeNote: In an intrinsic semiconductor, nₑ = nₕ (equal number of electrons and holes).
questions.answer: **Intrinsic semiconductor:** a **chemically pure** semiconductor (pure Si or Ge) whose charge carriers arise **only from thermal excitation** across the small band gap — each excited electron leaves one hole, so electrons and holes exist in **equal numbers** (n_e = n_h = n_i), and conductivity is low and strongly temperature-dependent. **Electrons (as carriers):** negative charge carriers — electrons thermally promoted from the valence band into the conduction band, free to drift under a field; their motion constitutes ordinary current. **Holes:** positive charge carriers — the **vacancies** left in the valence band when electrons are excited out; a neighbouring valence electron can fall into the vacancy, moving the 'hole' in the opposite direction, so the hole behaves exactly like a mobile **positive charge** (+e). **Deep point:** the hole is not a missing electron 'flying around' — it is the collective motion of valence electrons filling vacancies, which the mathematics treats perfectly as a positive particle; two carriers per excitation, moving opposite ways, adding to the same conventional current.

questions.question: Differentiate between an elastic body and a plastic body.
questions.solution:
**Elastic body:**
- After the deforming force is removed, the body **regains its original size and shape** completely.
- Deformation is **reversible** and the limit of elasticity is not crossed.
- The restoring force lies within the elastic limit, so $F \propto x$ (Hooke's law).
- Property is measured by the **elastic modulus** (Young's modulus).
- Examples: steel, rubber (up to elastic limit), quartz, glass fibre.

**Plastic body:**
- After the deforming force is removed, the body **does not** regain its original shape and size; it keeps a **permanent deformation**.
- Deformation is **irreversible** and the elastic limit has been crossed.
- The limit of elasticity is small, e.g. $0.5\ \text{mm/m}$ for putty.
- Examples: putty, wet clay, wax, chewing gum, dough.

**Note:** Plastic deformation is essential in shaping metals by rolling, forging and bending.
questions.knowledgeNote: An elastic body regains its original shape after removing the deforming force; a plastic body keeps permanent deformation.
questions.answer: **Elastic body:** recovers its **original shape and size completely** when the deforming force is removed — obeys Hooke's law within the elastic limit (e.g. steel spring, quartz fibre); deformation is reversible and the stress–strain path retraces itself. **Plastic body:** does **not** recover — it retains a permanent (irreversible) deformation after the force is removed (e.g. clay, putty, lead); it has no well-defined elastic limit and flows under sustained stress. **Differences:** (1) reversible vs permanent deformation; (2) elastic bodies store the work of deformation as recoverable strain energy, plastic bodies dissipate it as heat; (3) real materials are elastic up to a **yield point** and plastic beyond it — the distinction is a matter of regime, not of substance. **Deep point:** putty and steel are the same atoms in different regimes — every material has an elastic range and a plastic range; the 'body' label describes which regime you are operating it in.
